facts.claim: "Chase the Feeling" is a cover of a Kris Kristofferson song. Kristofferson first released it in 2006, and The Devil Makes Three put it on Redemption & Ruin in 2016.
It is track 4 on Redemption & Ruin, a 12-song covers record released on New West Records on September 16, 2016.

The song's credits list Jerry Roe on drums, Dan Dugmore on pedal steel guitar, Bobby Wood on organ and Lucia Turino on upright bass. Cooper McBean is listed on vocals and Pete Bernhard on background vocals.
The album is credited as produced by The Devil Makes Three, with David Ferguson as associate producer and recording engineer. David Shipley mastered it.
The album was recorded at The Butcher Shoppe in Nashville, TN, and mastered at Foxwood Mastering in Nashville.
The band recorded the album live at Dave Ferguson's Butcher Shoppe studio instead of multi-tracking it, according to PopMatters. Bernhard says most tracks were cut live with the guest musicians.
Pete Bernhard said guests such as Jerry Douglas effectively co-produced songs by contributing ideas, and that the band recorded most tracks live with them.
Bernhard described the album as one side redemption and one side ruin. He said it collects songs by heroes who inspired the band, intended to show listeners where the band comes from.

The album's first half deals with the faults and vices that drive creation in music, and the second half deals with absolution and forgiveness. Its covers range from blues (Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters) to country (Townes Van Zandt, Hank Williams Sr.), gospel, bluegrass and Tom Waits.

Redemption & Ruin is the band's only covers album and their fifth release (second for New West). The band started in Olympia, WA, and moved to Santa Cruz, CA. Their earlier album I'm a Stranger Here (2013) was produced by Buddy Miller.

research.lineage: The Devil Makes Three blend bluegrass, folk, country, blues and rockabilly into an old-time string-band sound, and Redemption & Ruin pays tribute to the blues, gospel, country and bluegrass figures who shaped them.

draft:
"Ain't you handsome when you're high?" is a compliment with a knife in it. On **Chase The Feeling**, The Devil Makes Three set that question over a loping shuffle, and the easy swing of the groove makes it cut deeper. The song is Kris Kristofferson's, first released by him in 2006. The band placed it fourth on Redemption & Ruin, the covers record Pete Bernhard described as one side redemption and one side ruin. This one sits on the ruin side, among songs about the vices that drive people to make music in the first place.

What keeps it from turning into a sermon is the opening line: "Takes one, to know one, I know how you feel." The narrator isn't standing on clean ground. Everything after it, the scorn and the pity, comes from someone who knows those demons and has watched them drag a friend down the hallways of his own brain. Kinship and contempt sit side by side, and the song never lets one cancel the other. The middle verse becomes a run of bitter permissions, each "let it" pushing the damage further from the user, until "Let it run your children off" hands the bill to people who never chose any of this. Then comes the flattest line in the song. He knows better, the narrator says, he just doesn't care. It sounds less like an accusation than like exhaustion.

The last verse drifts into midnight and a lover whose eyes look older than she is. It ends with the narrator wondering how this man is still alive, a line caught halfway between awe and dread. The doubled chorus at the close could read as filler. Instead it plays like the habit itself, the same promise made twice.

Cooper McBean takes the lead, with a clear voice and a little rasp, and he sings conversationally, with no harmonies stacked behind him. So every line arrives one-on-one, like something said across a kitchen table. An acoustic guitar strums steadily over a walking bass line, and Lucia Turino is credited on upright. The banjo answers the vocal with quick runs between phrases, and the drums keep a simple, driving beat with the snare out front. The sound is dry and unpolished. The band cut most of the album live at The Butcher Shoppe in Nashville with David Ferguson engineering, and the credits add Jerry Roe on drums, Dan Dugmore on pedal steel, and Bobby Wood on organ. Bernhard said the record was meant to show where the band comes from. Here they take Kristofferson's blunt, plainspoken writing and run it through their old-time string-band sound, keeping it light on its feet when it could have dragged.

The song holds you in that uneasy spot where you love someone and can't stand watching them, and the bounce under it makes the disaster sound almost like a good time, which is exactly how it looks from the inside.
